title: Living ashtpadi 11
hookLine: trust and effort together: act, and leave the rest

cards: Punjab is farming country, and a farmer there knows something in his bones that the rest of us learn slowly. You plow. You choose good seed and sow it at the right time, straight and deep.

You watch the canal, pull the weeds, get up before dawn for months. And then you wait for rain you cannot make, sun you cannot order, and a harvest never entirely yours to decide. A lazy farmer has nothing to harvest.
A farmer who thinks he controls the sky wears himself out. The good farmer does both: works, and lets go.

teach.b: For three days ashtpadi eleven has said God is the doer of all. Karan kaaran, the cause of causes. Jo tis bhaavai soee hog, whatever pleases Him comes to pass.
Nothing outside the hukam. Heard alone, that could sound like a reason to sit on the porch. Sikh teaching doesn't read it that way.
Guru Arjan, who wrote Sukhmani, wrote a couplet elsewhere in the Guru Granth Sahib: make the effort, and live; earn, and enjoy peace; meditate, and meet God; Nanak, then anxiety is gone.
The word for effort is udam: striving, enterprise, getting up and doing. So the Sikh picture has two hands.

teach.h: ONE HAND WORKS, ONE HAND OPENS.
teach.b: One works: udam, honest labor, what Sikhs call kirat karni, earning by your own effort. The other opens: bhaana, trust, leaving the outcome to the doer of all. Neither hand alone is the path.
Effort without trust becomes anxiety, gripping the wheel of the whole road. Trust without effort becomes an excuse.
Together they give what the couplet promises: anxiety is gone. Not because everything works out, but because you did your part fully and stopped carrying the part that was never yours.
Like the farmer: plow as if it all depends on you, then look at the sky as if it all depends on God.

how: Sikhs hold kirat karni, honest effort and work, together with accepting God's will, and teachers quote Guru Arjan's couplet on udam, effort, as the balance between the two.

o: effort, getting up and doing the work
waiting calmly for God to act for you
a prayer said before starting a task

p: plows, then looks at the sky

s: 'God is the doer' means Sikhs should sit back and wait
Guru Arjan also wrote: make the effort, and live.
Guru Arjan's couplet on udam ends with anxiety gone
make the effort, earn, meditate: Nanak, anxiety is gone.
trust without effort is the Sikh ideal
the Sikh picture has two hands: one works, one opens.

games.q: you're a Punjabi farmer at sowing time. by ashtpadi eleven and Guru Arjan's couplet, what do you do?
o: sow nothing; the rain will decide anyway.
plow and sow with all your effort, then trust the sky.
stay up every night worrying about the rain.
games.why: udam and bhaana together: act fully, then release the part that was never yours.

practice: Picture one task in front of you today and see yourself doing it fully, hands busy, giving it real effort. Then picture it done, the email sent, the meal served, and open your hands, palms up, like a farmer looking at the sky.
Breathe in: I act; breathe out: I release; and if you pray, offer the result to Waheguru.

wordCard.voice: Udam, effort, striving. Trust and effort together: udam with one hand, bhaana with the other. Act, and leave the rest.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: udam, effort, striving; Guru Arjan's couplet pairs it with trust in God.

carryVoice: Your line: act, then release. One hand works and one hand opens, like the farmer's. That's day four hundred eighty-one.

sources.work: Guru Granth Sahib (Guru Arjan, Gauri Sukhmani)
